summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors. On 4 October 2023 the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838, which had provided for penal servitude of up to five years for sodomy, ruling it unconstitutional and that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. Prosecutions under the section were rare; a same-sex couple was arrested under it in 2015, and the US State Department's 2016 country report recorded that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor rather than reaching same-sex couples in court.

Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, describes the repeal as an advance for lesbian, gay and bisexual people while recording that progress for trans and intersex people has been 'less evident'. No criminal provision identified in the sources targets gender expression, and no case is documented in which a visitor was prosecuted for presenting in clothing associated with another gender. The documented harm to trans people is social: the 2016 State Department report recorded the harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Mauritius. AfricLaw's analysis of 23 August 2024 identifies the Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition to trans Mauritians, concluding that legal recognition and protection remain inadequate. The Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief argues for administrative recognition and notes that the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders in 2019, calling on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law. Outright International confirms that legal gender recognition is not possible.

Discrimination protection covers sexual orientation but not gender identity: the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination. No same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised. Intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Public hostility is documented but met with state protection. Pride has been held since 2005 and draws counter-protesters; in 2018 the march was cancelled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, though police had earlier deployed to protect marchers and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. During the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

Access to care is uneven. According to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form, and LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, though anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. LGBTI people facing verbal abuse or violence in the family generally reported to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and the Young Queer Alliance rather than to police.

Visibility has increased: Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan became the first transgender woman to participate in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024, an AfricLaw-documented milestone set against pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Mauritius stands apart from much of the region in the direction of its legal trajectory: Section 250 was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2023 after the government said in 2017 it would not repeal the section and a decriminalisation bill by former Attorney General Rama Valayden failed to pass. A constitutional challenge filed in October 2019 by young people, supported by the Young Queer Alliance, the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek and Collectif Arc-en-Ciel, preceded the ruling.

Public opinion appears comparatively tolerant by regional standards. A 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour, and polls indicate Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries, with acceptance growing particularly among the younger generation. Religious leaders including Cardinal Maurice Piat condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest in 2018 and called for tolerance, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.

The gap between decriminalisation and recognition is the defining pattern: same-sex conduct is no longer criminal, but trans Mauritians still cannot change legal gender, LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no partnership recognition exists. The 2024 Miss Universe Mauritius participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan raised visibility without altering the underlying legal position.
localsOnly:
Trans Mauritians face a structural recognition barrier rather than a criminal one. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database govern identity documents, and no administrative route to change gender marker exists; the Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief sets out the case for administrative recognition and cites the WHO's ICD-11 removal of trans categories from mental disorders in 2019.

Resident-facing support runs through civil society. Collectif Arc-en-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016 when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians, engaging in support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns, and Association VISA-G is active on trans issues. LGBTI people facing family verbal abuse or violence generally reported to these local NGOs.

Discrimination in employment is addressed by the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019, which cover sexual orientation. Intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, though nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned. Hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals according to the government, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form, and LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals. Since 2014 men who have sex with men have been permitted to donate blood, though anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. LGBTI organisations cannot register.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2023 Supreme Court ruling on Section 250 has produced any change in police practice toward trans people presenting in clothing associated with another gender is not sourced; no enforcement data post-dating the judgment appears in the inventory.

The extent to which the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 cover gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is unresolved in the sources, which describe the protection in sexual-orientation terms only.

Claims about the current availability and cost of gender-affirming care in Mauritius rest on a Wikipedia-sourced summary of a government statement and are not independently corroborated in the inventory; the same applies to reports that LGBTQI persons have occasionally been turned away from blood donation despite the 2014 policy change.

The inventory contains no entry or visa rules, no screening procedures at immigration that might affect trans travellers, and no data on how Mauritian consulates abroad handle gender marker changes on passports. These are not sourced either way.
